one_liner: Indirect sort wrapper: sorts indices or pointers, then permutes once; beats std::sort on structs over ~152 bytes.
what_it_does: plf::indiesort is a header-only wrapper that lets std::sort (or any random-access sort) run on non-random-access ranges such as std::list or a forward-iterator container, and speeds up sorting of large element types in vectors and arrays. The API mirrors std::sort: indiesort(first, last[, comp]), indiesort(container[, comp]), plus a (first, last, comp, size) overload that skips std::distance. For random-access ranges with elements under 152 bytes it simply forwards to std::sort, so it can be used everywhere without a size check at the call site.
how_it_is_fast: It is an indirect sort (argsort) followed by in-place permutation by cycle-following. For random-access ranges it fills an array of the smallest unsigned type that can hold N (unsigned char up to 255 elements, then unsigned short, unsigned int, size_t), sorts those indices with a comparator that dereferences first + index, then walks each permutation cycle so every element is moved about once instead of the O(N log N) moves std::sort makes; with 496-byte elements the move traffic dominates, so cheap index swaps win. For non-random-access ranges it sorts an array of {element pointer, original index} pairs the same way, or, for elements no bigger than two pointers, copies them into a contiguous array, sorts that and copies back.
when_to_use: Sorting a std::vector, std::deque or C array of large structs (well above 152 bytes) where moving an element costs far more than comparing two keys
Element types that are expensive or non-trivial to move or copy, where one move per element beats std::sort's repeated swaps
Sorting std::list, std::forward_list, plf::colony/hive or other non-random-access containers of small to medium types (under ~272 bytes) faster than list::sort, or where no member sort exists at all
Codebases stuck on C++98/03 that still want a generic indirect sort; it is also a ready-made argsort harness for plugging in pdqsort or another sort through the PLF_SORT_FUNCTION macro
when_not_to_use: Arrays of built-in or small types: below 152 bytes it just calls std::sort, so a SIMD or radix sort (vqsort, x86-simd-sort, pdqsort, spreadsort) is the place to look for speed

When stability matters: the default inner sort is std::sort on indices, so equal elements end in unspecified order (std::list::sort is stable); define PLF_SORT_FUNCTION as std::stable_sort if you need it
std::list of types larger than ~272 bytes: the author's own figures say list::sort (which only relinks nodes) is faster there, and indiesort does not switch to it automatically

Memory-tight or allocation-sensitive paths: every non-trivial call heap-allocates N indices (random access) or N pointer+size_t pairs (list path) through std::allocator, ignoring the container's allocator

Code that holds iterators, references or pointers into a std::list across the sort: indiesort moves values between nodes rather than relinking them, so those handles end up pointing at different values

integration.form: header-only (plf_indiesort.h plus the shared plf_tools.h and plf_tools_undef.h shipped in the repo); also packaged as vcpkg port plf-indiesort 1.4.10 (depends on plf-tools) and Conan Center plf_indiesort (up to 1.41)
integration.dependencies: none outside the standard library; needs the bundled plf_tools.h
integration.min_toolchain: C++98 per the README (C++98/03/11/14/etc-compatible); plf_tools.h enables move semantics and type traits from C++11 and constexpr functions from C++20 (GCC 12+/Clang 15+ with matching libstdc++/libc++, or MSVC 19.29+)
integration.platforms: any: portable standard C++, no intrinsics or architecture-specific code in the sort itself
integration.thread_safety: not documented; it is a stateless function template with no globals, so concurrent calls on disjoint ranges are safe, but the caller must not touch the range during the sort
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same (first, last[, comp]) shape as std::sort and identical results up to the order of equal keys, but it allocates a temporary index array and is not a replacement for std::list::sort semantics (unstable, values move between nodes, element type must be move- or copy-assignable)

gotchas: Not stable by default: ties come out in std::sort's unspecified order. Swapping the inner sort is a compile-time macro (define PLF_SORT_FUNCTION before including the header), so it applies to every indiesort call in that translation unit.

On std::list it reassigns element values across existing nodes instead of relinking them, unlike list::sort, so outstanding iterators and references now see different values and the element type must be assignable.

Scratch buffers are raw std::allocator allocations with no RAII: a throwing comparator leaks the index array, and a throwing move during the permutation phase also leaves one element moved-from. In the small-element list path, moved-from temporaries are deallocated without their destructors being run when the type is nothrow-move-assignable but not trivially copy-assignable.

The 152-byte switch to plain std::sort is a hard-coded constant taken from the author's Haswell + GCC runs; on other CPUs, compilers or element layouts the real crossover may differ, and the repo ships no benchmark code to re-measure it (the test suite only checks sortedness, not that the multiset of elements is preserved).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick indiesort over pdqsort, x86-simd-sort or vqsort when elements are large, opaque structs compared through an arbitrary comparator, or when the container is not random-access; those siblings target built-in keys or contiguous arrays, while indiesort cuts the element-move cost and can wrap pdqsort itself through PLF_SORT_FUNCTION. If the key is a single 32- or 64-bit field and the target is x86, x86-simd-sort's object_qsort (also an argsort, with SIMD) is likely faster.
verified_claims_summary: The README says indiesort averages +146% (about 2.46x) faster than std::sort on vectors or arrays of 496-byte structs and +28% faster than std::list::sort for types under 272 bytes, with crossovers at 152 bytes (vs std::sort) and 272 bytes (vs list::sort); a 2020 announcement quoted +130% on ~480-byte structs. These are first-party averages over unspecified element counts on a Haswell machine with GCC (from a search snippet of the blocked plflib.org pages), with no compiler version, flags or CPU model, and the benchmark code is not in the repo; the test suite's large_struct is exactly 496 bytes on 64-bit, so it probably matches the benchmarked type.
status_note: Actively maintained by its single author (51 commits, v1.4.10 in July 2026, plf_tools updates through 2026-10-03; both GitHub issues closed), Zlib-licensed and three small headers, so trivial to vendor or pull from vcpkg/Conan; usability is copyable but the speed numbers are first-party only and cannot be rerun from the repo.
sources_read: WebSearch snippet: plf::indiesort benchmark, Haswell GCC (+130% on ~480-byte structs, plflib.org/benchmarks_haswell_gcc.htm#sort)
